subject: Critical Thinking
title: Abduction: Inference to the Best Explanation
description: A short lesson to help you apply Abduction: Inference to the Best Explanation.

hook.text: You wake up and the streets are wet. It probably rained. You didn't deduce or induce — you abduced.

buildup.text: Abductive reasoning picks the best explanation for an observation from competing possibilities.

discovery.text: Charles Peirce coined it in the 1890s. It's how doctors diagnose, detectives solve, and scientists hypothesize.

twist.text: The 'best' explanation isn't necessarily true. It's just the simplest one that fits all the facts — so far.

climax.text: Sherlock Holmes didn't do deduction. His famous method was abduction — inference to the best explanation.

punchline.text: Eliminate the impossible. Whatever remains is probably true.

quiz.question: What type of reasoning did Sherlock Holmes actually use?
options: Abduction — inference to the best explanation

details.summary: Abductive reasoning selects the best available explanation for a set of observations, even when certainty is impossible. It is the logic behind medical diagnoses, detective work, and scientific hypothesis formation.
details.whyItMatters: Most real-world reasoning is abductive—we constantly choose the most plausible explanation and act on it without waiting for certainty.
takeaways: Abduction picks the best explanation from competing hypotheses
It is weaker than deduction but essential for practical decisions
Simplicity, scope, and testability make one explanation better than another

faq.question: How does abductive reasoning differ from inductive reasoning?
faq.answer: Induction generalizes from repeated observations. Abduction selects the best explanation for a specific set of observations, even from a single case.

faq.question: What criteria determine the best explanation in abductive reasoning?
faq.answer: Simplicity, explanatory power, consistency with known facts, testability, and the ability to predict new observations all contribute to ranking competing explanations.
